profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting in an ML systems lab between the faculty lead for reproducibility infrastructure and the research engineer maintaining benchmark automation. They are preparing a refreshed internal showcase based on the SysML'19 Collective Knowledge demo so it can be shown to visiting collaborators in four weeks and then repurposed for artifact-evaluation training. The agenda is to decide what it means to get the old demo working again on current lab hardware, what should go into the collaborator-facing artifact bundle, how much to modernize the execution environment, who owns packaging versus demo prep, and what must be validated before the visit. The expected outcome is a concrete work split for updating the CK pipelines, validating a representative subset of workloads, and assembling a reusable demo package.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.role: Principal Investigator for ML Systems Reproducibility
members.expertise: ML systems, benchmarking methodology, artifact evaluation
members.background: Leads a university lab that studies repeatable benchmarking across hardware and software stacks and has served on several systems and ML artifact-evaluation committees.
members.private_state: Wants a polished, low-risk demo that reliably runs during the collaborator visit and can later be pointed to as a lab reproducibility asset, while avoiding a month-long infrastructure rewrite that delays other lab deadlines.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'get the SysML'19 demo working again,' they usually mean restoring the audience-facing flow on the lab's current workstation setup, not reconstructing every historical execution condition.

An 'artifact bundle' for a guided collaborator demo naturally means commands, pinned CK entries, a short README, and exported plots or tables, not extra evaluator-facing checking utilities unless requested.
Validation is satisfied if the selected workflows run cleanly and preserve the same qualitative trade-offs and story as the original demo, even if absolute numbers move on newer hardware.
If they 'modernize the environment just enough,' the practical path is to patch the existing workstation image and CK metadata rather than introducing a new bootstrap mechanism.
Giving the engineer ownership of 'packaging' ordinarily includes final demo-readiness details like cleanup of instructions and handoff materials.

members.name: Alexei Petrov
members.role: Senior Research Engineer for Experiment Infrastructure
members.expertise: CK workflows, benchmark automation, systems tooling, reproducible execution
members.background: Previously maintained benchmarking pipelines for an industrial research group and has extensive hands-on experience reviving older CK-based workflows on newer toolchains.
members.private_state: Wants this refresh to eliminate fragile lab-specific assumptions so the package is genuinely reusable by future students and artifact evaluators, and worries that a presentation-only fix will create another brittle one-off demo.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'get the SysML'19 demo working again,' the responsible interpretation is to make the workflow runnable in a way that an external technical user could retrace without undocumented lab fixes.

An 'artifact bundle' normally includes evaluator-facing support files such as hardware detection helpers, sanity-check scripts, and result parsers so someone can verify what they ran, even if environment setup is handled separately.
Validation only really counts if refreshed outputs are checked against archived reference runs closely enough to identify and explain drift caused by version changes.
If they 'modernize the environment just enough,' the least risky method is to create a scripted or containerized bootstrap path from a clean machine instead of relying on a tuned workstation image.
Ownership of 'packaging' is primarily about repository structure and executable support assets; presentation polish and walkthrough framing remain with the PI unless explicitly reassigned.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to get the demo working again
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both talk about 'getting the SysML'19 demo working again.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means restoring a smooth end-to-end demo experience for a few representative CK workflows on the lab's current standard workstation so visitors can see the original narrative and outcomes.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means making the old workflow runnable again in a technically faithful, externally reusable sense, with enough traceability that another engineer could rerun the same structure without hidden lab fixes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds operational rather than methodological, so it feels like ordinary planning shorthand; each hears a reasonable, role-consistent default and has no reason to suspect the other is using a stricter or narrower meaning.

misalignment_points.topic: What belongs in the artifact bundle
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to prepare 'the artifact bundle' for collaborators.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the bundle consists of the curated demo repository, concise instructions, pinned CK metadata, sample commands, and exported result summaries suitable for a guided showcase.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the bundle also includes evaluator-facing support tooling such as hardware detection scripts, automated sanity checks, and log/result parsers so an outside user can verify that the run behaved as expected.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are used to the phrase from reproducibility work, and the extra support tooling feels to M2 like an obvious part of any serious artifact, while to M1 it feels like optional implementation detail rather than a scope boundary worth naming.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as validation before the visit
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the refreshed workflows should be 'validated before the visit.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes validation means confirming that the selected demo paths execute successfully on the lab workstation and still show the same qualitative speed-accuracy or software-hardware trade-off patterns as the original materials.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes validation means comparing refreshed runs against archived SysML'19-era outputs and documenting deviations beyond a relatively tight tolerance so any drift is explicitly explained.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Validation is standard professional language and both participants expect some version drift in revived benchmarks, so the hidden difference is not whether to validate but the threshold for what evidence is sufficient.

misalignment_points.topic: How to modernize the environment just enough
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'modernize the environment just enough' so the pipelines run next month.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes Alexei will make targeted fixes to the existing lab workstation image, update CK entries where needed, and keep the setup lightweight so the team can move quickly.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes he will build a scripted or containerized bootstrap path from a clean machine, because that is the minimal reliable method for reviving an old benchmark stack without hidden dependencies.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'just enough' signals pragmatism to both of them, but they map pragmatism to different default execution methods based on their roles: minimal visible change for M1, minimal hidden fragility for M2.

If it runs reliably for the visit and can later serve as a polished reproducibility asset, that's the win. I do not want this to become a month-long infrastructure rewrite.
